section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About MSI and MSI-H
section.intro: MSI (microsatellite instability) and MSI-H (MSI-high) are biomarkers found on tumor test reports that can help predict whether immunotherapy may work across many cancer types. These FAQs explain what the terms mean, how testing is done, and what MSI-H results may mean for treatment planning.

items.q: What is MSI in a cancer report?
items.a: MSI, or microsatellite instability, is a biomarker that shows how well a tumor can repair mistakes in its DNA. Microsatellites are short, repeated DNA sequences, and instability means these repeats have changed in length because the cell's mismatch repair system is not working properly. MSI is reported from tumor tissue or genetic testing and helps oncologists understand tumor behavior and possible treatment options, including immunotherapy in selected patients.

MSI-H, or microsatellite instability-high, means a tumor shows a high level of DNA repair errors due to a faulty mismatch repair system. This creates many genetic changes that can make the cancer more visible to the immune system. MSI-H tumors may respond better to immunotherapy in selected patients, though results depend on cancer type, stage, overall health, and specialist review. Final treatment decisions should be made by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is the difference between MSI-H and dMMR?
items.a: MSI-H and dMMR describe the same underlying problem measured in two different ways. dMMR, or deficient mismatch repair, is detected by immunohistochemistry testing that looks for missing repair proteins, while MSI-H is identified by PCR or genetic sequencing that measures unstable DNA repeats. In most cases the results agree, so reports may list either term. Both suggest a tumor that may be considered for immunotherapy after specialist assessment.

items.q: Why is MSI-H called a biomarker across all cancers?
items.a: MSI-H is considered a tumor-agnostic biomarker because it can appear in many different cancer types, not just one organ. Regulatory approvals allow certain immunotherapy drugs to be used based on MSI-H status regardless of where the cancer started, such as colon, endometrial, stomach, or other tumors. This means treatment eligibility may depend on the biomarker itself, though final decisions still depend on the full clinical picture and specialist review.

items.q: Which cancers are most often MSI-H?
items.a: MSI-H is most commonly found in colorectal and endometrial (uterine) cancers, but it can also appear in stomach, small bowel, ovarian, prostate, pancreatic, and other tumors. It is more frequent in cancers linked to Lynch syndrome, an inherited condition affecting DNA repair. Because MSI-H can occur across many cancer types, testing is increasingly recommended, though whether to test depends on cancer type, stage, and the treating team's advice.

items.q: How is MSI or MSI-H testing done?
items.a: MSI and MSI-H testing is usually done on a sample of tumor tissue from a biopsy or surgery. Common methods include immunohistochemistry (IHC) to check mismatch repair proteins, PCR testing to compare DNA repeat lengths, and next-generation sequencing that can detect MSI alongside other biomarkers. Some blood-based tests may also assess MSI. The right method depends on the tumor type, available sample, and laboratory, and should be guided by the oncology team.

items.q: Who should get MSI or MSI-H testing?
items.a: MSI testing may be considered for patients with colorectal, endometrial, and several other cancers, especially advanced or metastatic disease where immunotherapy could be an option. It is also used to screen for Lynch syndrome, which can affect family members. Guidelines increasingly support broad testing, but whether it is right for a specific patient depends on cancer type, stage, previous treatment, and specialist review. The treating team decides when testing is appropriate.

items.q: Is MSI-H testing safe and does it require extra procedures?
items.a: MSI-H testing is generally safe because it is performed in the laboratory on tissue that has already been collected during a biopsy or surgery. In most cases no additional procedure is needed, so there is little added risk to the patient. If no suitable sample is available, a new biopsy or a blood-based test may be suggested. Your oncology team can explain what sample is needed and how testing fits your care plan.

items.q: Does MSI-H mean immunotherapy will definitely work?
items.a: An MSI-H result does not guarantee that immunotherapy will work, but it may improve the chance of benefit in selected patients. MSI-H tumors often respond better to immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet responses vary and some patients may not benefit. Treatment success depends on cancer type, stage, overall health, prior therapy, and other factors. Immunotherapy also carries potential side effects, so decisions should be discussed carefully with a qualified oncology team.

items.q: How much does MSI or MSI-H testing cost?
items.a: The cost of MSI or MSI-H testing varies widely depending on the method used, the laboratory, and the country. Simple IHC or PCR testing is usually less expensive, while next-generation sequencing panels that include MSI and other biomarkers cost more. Final pricing depends on the hospital, the tests ordered, and whether it is part of a larger genomic panel. Your care team or CancerFax can help you request an estimated cost.

items.q: Is MSI-H testing available in India?
items.a: MSI-H testing is available in India at many major cancer hospitals and specialized molecular pathology laboratories. Testing options include IHC for mismatch repair proteins, PCR-based MSI testing, and next-generation sequencing panels. Availability and turnaround time can vary between centers, and some samples may be sent to reference laboratories. Whether a specific test is suitable depends on the tumor type and specialist advice, and the treating team can confirm local options.

items.q: Which countries offer MSI-H testing and MSI-guided immunotherapy?
items.a: MSI-H testing and MSI-guided immunotherapy are available in many countries with established cancer care, including India, China, the United States, and several others. Access to specific immunotherapy drugs depends on local regulatory approvals, hospital availability, and treatment protocols. Some patients travel abroad for testing, second opinions, or therapy, though access is never guaranteed. Decisions about where to test or treat should follow specialist review and comparison of options.

items.q: Which immunotherapy drugs are used for MSI-H cancers?
items.a: Immune checkpoint inhibitors are the main class of drugs used for MSI-H cancers, and examples include pembrolizumab, nivolumab, and dostarlimab in various settings. Some MSI-H tumors are treated with these drugs regardless of where the cancer started, based on the biomarker. Availability, approved uses, and combinations differ by country and cancer type. Whether a specific drug may be suitable depends on the full clinical picture and the treating oncology team's assessment.

items.q: Are there clinical trials for MSI-H tumors?
items.a: Yes, there are clinical trials studying new immunotherapies, drug combinations, and treatment sequences for MSI-H and dMMR tumors. These trials may explore options for different cancer types and stages, including situations where standard treatment has stopped working. Enrollment is not guaranteed and depends on strict inclusion and exclusion criteria assessed after medical record review and investigator evaluation. Your oncology team can help identify trials that may match your diagnosis.

items.q: Can MSI-H immunotherapy be used before surgery?
items.a: In some MSI-H cancers, immunotherapy may be considered before surgery, an approach called neoadjuvant treatment, particularly in selected colorectal and other tumors under study. Early research suggests some patients respond strongly, but this use is still being evaluated and is not appropriate for everyone. Eligibility depends on cancer type, stage, overall health, and specialist judgment. Any decision to use immunotherapy before surgery should be made by an experienced multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: What reports are needed to review MSI-H status for treatment abroad?
items.a: To review MSI-H status for treatment abroad, doctors usually need the pathology report, MSI or dMMR test results, and any next-generation sequencing or biomarker reports. Recent imaging scans, a treatment summary, and details of previous therapies are also helpful. Having complete and clear reports allows a faster and more accurate second opinion. CancerFax or your care team can guide you on collecting the documents needed for specialist review.

items.q: How can international patients access MSI-guided immunotherapy?
items.a: International patients can access MSI-guided immunotherapy by first confirming MSI-H or dMMR status, then seeking a second opinion from a hospital that offers the relevant treatment. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, drug availability, visa approval, travel fitness, and the patient's condition. None of these steps is guaranteed. Careful planning of reports, cost estimates, appointments, and follow-up care helps, and final treatment decisions rest with the treating oncology team.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with MSI and MSI-H?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support related to MSI and MSI-H testing or immunotherapy. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health. CancerFax does not guarantee test results, hospital acceptance, treatment access, or specific outcomes.
